title: Fiber Bundle Fault Tolerance of GKP Codes
authors: Ansgar G. Burchards; Steven T. Flammia; Jonathan Conrad
abstract: We investigate multi-mode GKP (Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill) quantum error-correcting codes from a geometric perspective. First, we construct their moduli space as a quotient of groups and exhibit it as a fiber bundle over the moduli space of symplectically integral lattices. We then establish the Gottesman–Zhang conjecture for logical GKP Clifford operations, showing that all such gates arise from parallel transport with respect to a flat connection on this space. Specifically, non-trivial Clifford operations correspond to topologically non-contractible paths on the space of GKP codes, while logical identity operations correspond to contractible paths.

                                                        We investigate multi-mode GKP (Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill) quantum error-
                                                    correcting codes from a geometric perspective. First, we construct their moduli
                                                    space as a quotient of groups and exhibit it as a fiber bundle over the moduli
                                                    space of symplectically integral lattices. We then establish the Gottesman–
                                                    Zhang conjecture for logical GKP Clifford operations, showing that all such
                                                    gates arise from parallel transport with respect to a flat connection on this
                                                    space. Specifically, non-trivial Clifford operations correspond to topologically
                                                    non-contractible paths on the space of GKP codes, while logical identity oper-
                                                    ations correspond to contractible paths.



                                           1 Introduction
                                           Quantum computers hold the promise of providing a speedup over classical computers on
                                           specific computational tasks such as factoring [1]. In order for quantum computers to realize
                                           this potential and perform arbitrarily large quantum computations, the key requirement,
                                           besides universality, is that of fault tolerance [1, 2, 3]. This means that given high enough
                                           control accuracy and sufficiently weak noise with sufficiently low correlations, arbitrarily
                                           long and precise computations are possible with only a modest cost in additional overhead.
                                           On a macroscopic level, it means that sufficiently good individual components are robust
                                           enough to suppress errors arbitrarily well when combined in the right way and in sufficient
                                           numbers.
                                               While a widely used, general, and intuitive concept, the term fault tolerance is often
                                           used in an ad-hoc fashion tailored to specific details of the context or platform under
                                           discussion. Three examples include transversal gates [4], which are fault-tolerant as they
                                           do not propagate errors; topological gates [5], implemented through the braiding of local-
                                           ized anyonic excitations on the ground space of a topological error-correcting code; and
                                           Gaussian unitary operations, which perform logical Clifford operations on GKP codes [6,
                                           7], with fault tolerance due to the fact that the relative increase of displacement errors is
                                           bounded. These different types of protocols span a variety of physical systems and con-
                                           ceptual frameworks, and while all three types of gates are sensibly deemed fault tolerant
                                           within their respective domains, they do not seem to arise from a single universal construc-
                                           tion method upon first inspection. For example, while the braiding of anyons is clearly
                                           topological in nature, this does not seem to be the case for either transversal or Gaussian
                                           unitary operations.


                                           Accepted in Quantum 2025-09-23, click title to verify. Published under CC-BY 4.0.                        1
    In their work [8], Gottesman and Zhang conjectured that in fact all types of fault-
tolerant gates can be regarded as topological, so that a universal perspective on fault
tolerance becomes possible. Here we prove the Gottesman–Zhang conjecture for logical
Clifford gates on multi-mode GKP codes by showing that they arise as the parallel transport
maps induced by a flat projective connection on a bundle over the space of all GKP codes.
Denoting by MGKP the manifold of all GKP stabilizer groups on n modes and by UG the
set of Gaussian unitary operators, we prove the following theorem.
Theorem 1.1. Any path C : [0, 1] → MGKP has a unique Gaussian unitary implementation
U : [0, 1] → UG /{eiϕ 1} with U (0) = 1 and C(t) = U (t)C(0)U † (t). Letting Gaussian uni-
taries act on the trivial bundle over MGKP with standard fiber the space R2n of displacement
operators as U C, D(ξ) = (U CU † , U D(ξ)U † ), then the associated connection is flat.
    Intuitively, implementing a path on a space of error correcting codes via some unitary
U (t) guarantees protection from errors at all times during gate implementation. Flatness
of the connection generating parallel transport both guarantees robustness to control in-
accuracies and that implemented logical gates are a feature of the path’s topology only.
The proof of Theorem 1.1 can be found in Section 6. To the best of our knowledge this is
the first proof of the Gottesman–Zhang conjecture for a multi-mode bosonic code; see also
Ref. [9] by the authors which provides a different perspective on the single-mode case.
    The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on
continuous variable quantum systems and lattice theory. In Section 3, we explore the
symmetry properties of symplectically integral lattices and derive an expression for their
moduli space. Section 4 reviews some background on GKP codes, formulated in lattice
theoretic language. Section 5 presents a construction of the GKP moduli space, while
Section 6 offers a proof of the Gottesman–Zhang conjecture for GKP Clifford operations.
We conclude in Section 7.


2 Preliminaries
In this section we introduce some preliminary notions regarding continuous variable quan-
tum systems, the theory of lattices, and quantum error correction. We also give a short
introduction to vector and fiber bundles in Appendix A. While we provide all necessary
background, we refer the interested reader to Refs. [7, 10] for additional background on
continuous variable physics, to Ref. [11] for a broad overview on lattice theory and to
Refs. [12, 13] for more detailed treatments of bundle theory.

2.2 Gaussian unitaries
Any unitary operator that is generated by a degree-2 polynomial in the position and mo-
mentum operators is called a Gaussian unitary. We denote the set of Gaussian unitaries by
UG and the Gaussian unitaries modulo phases by U G := UG /{eiϕ 1}. The full set U G is con-
veniently parametrized as Uη,S := D(η)Ŝ, where Ŝ denotes the metaplectic representation
of S ∈ Sp2n (R).

2.3 Metaplectic representation
The metaplectic representation is a double valued unitary representation of the symplectic
group Sp2n (R), up to factors of ±1. Formally this is a representation of the double cover
of Sp2n (R) whose values on the two branches differ by a factor of −1 [14]. We denote the
image of S ∈ Sp2n (R) under the metaplectic representation by Ŝ. All such Ŝ are Gaussian
unitaries and the representation satisfies the intertwining relation

                                              Ŝ † x̂Ŝ = S x̂ .                       (7)

From the definition of displacement operators one further obtains

                                           ŜD(ξ)Ŝ † = D(Sξ).                         (8)

2.4 Lattices
Throughout we will make extensive use of the concept of a lattice.

Definition 2.1 (Lattice). A lattice L is a discrete, additive subgroup of a vector space.

    We will exclusively consider lattices contained within some symplectic vector space V
and define the rank of a lattice as the dimension of the space spanned by its constituent
vectors. A lattice is called full rank if rank(L) = dim(V ).

Definition 2.3 (Gram Matrix). The Gram matrix associated to a lattice generator M is

    It can been shown that the Gram matrix of every lattice can be brought into standard

Definition 2.4. A Gram matrix A is said to be in standard form if A = J2 ⊗ D where
D is a diagonal matrix with positive integer entries, which are non-increasing along the

    This standard form was already introduced in the original paper [6] and classifies lattices
up to symplectic equivalence [15]. A drawback of this standard form, however, is that it
is not unique for any given symplectically integral lattice. In order to remedy this we
introduce a unique version of the standard form in Section 3.

2.5 Error-correcting codes
A quantum error correcting code is a subspace of a Hilbert space satisfying the Knill–
Laflamme conditions, which pertain to the protection of encoded information from noise
[16]. A common and useful way of defining such codes is through a set of stabilizing
operators.
Definition 2.5 (Stabilizer Code). Given a set of operators {O1 , . . . , On } we call the joint
eigenspace                      n                         o
                            C = |ψ⟩ ∈ H ∀i : Oi |ψ⟩ = |ψ⟩                                  (11)
the stabilizer code associated to the set of operators. The group S = ⟨O1 , . . . , On ⟩ is called
a stabilizer of the code.
    In most treatments of qubit stabilizer codes the operators Oi are restricted to be drawn
from the Pauli group, leading to a class of highly structured codes. Analogously, GKP codes
are stabilizer codes stabilized by displacement operators. As we are interested in idealized
GKP codes, whose member states are formally of infinite energy, we choose to define GKP
codes indirectly through their stabilizer groups.
Definition 2.6. A GKP code is specified by a stabilizer of the form

    The phase components ϕi are commonly suppressed in the literature since important
error correction properties, such as distance and encoded logical dimension of the resulting
code, are independent of them. However, since we aim to fully parametrize the set of all
existing GKP codes it is necessary to explicitly include them here. The requirement for
the set L to form a lattice is a direct consequence of the fact that the stabilizer forms
a group and integrality follows from the requirement that its elements must be mutually
commuting. Demanding the lattice L to be full rank is equivalent to encoding only a finite
dimensional quantum system as opposed to a full mode. The close connection between
GKP codes and lattices has already been discussed in the original work [6] as well as more
recently in Refs. [15, 17, 18, 19]. We now turn to discuss some of the theory of lattices
before returning to GKP codes in Section 4.


3 Symplectic automorphism groups and moduli space of lattices
Given a lattice L, any symplectic transformation on the embedding vector space results in
another lattice SL. Two lattices related by such a transformation are said to be symplec-
tically equivalent. The set of such transformations preserving a given lattice is known as
its associated symplectic automorphism group, given by
                                             n                          o
                               AutS (L) := S ∈ Sp2n (R) SL = L .                        (13)

The automorphism group is directly related to logical Clifford operations on GKP codes,
as we will discuss in Section 4.2. We are here interested in the structure of the moduli
space Sp2n (R)/AutS (L) of lattices symplectically equivalent to a given lattice L. We begin
by determining the structure of the automorphism group for an arbitrary full rank lattice.

3.1 Structure of symplectic automorphism groups
Let M be a generator of a full rank lattice L. Under a symplectic operation S the generator
matrix transforms to M S T and thus yields the original lattice exactly if this too is a

    We will see below that non-identity Clifford gates on GKP codes arise from non-
contractible loops in Mlat . While the space Mlat is in general high-dimensional, in
the single-mode case its connected components are the 3-dimensional quotient spaces
Sp2 (R)/Sp2 (Z) which are topologically equivalent to a 3-sphere with a trefoil knot γ re-
moved [21]. We illustrate this space in Fig. 1 and refer the interested reader to references [21,
22] for more details on the topology of this space. Clifford gates on single-mode GKP codes
can then be seen to arise from non-contractible loops that interlink nontrivially with the
trefoil knot. We also note that the first homotopy group of S 3 − γ is given by B3 , the
braid group on three strands. The construction hence also yields a homomorphism from
this braid group to the Clifford group modulo Paulis.


4 GKP codes
We now return to the topic of GKP codes. Their connection to the theory of lattices
originates from the form of their stabilizer groups which we recall here.
Definition 2.6. A GKP code is specified by a stabilizer of the form
                                       D                               E
                                 S = eiϕ1 D(ξ1 ), . . . , eiϕ2n D(ξ2n )                     (12)

where the set L = ξ ∈ R2n | ∃ϕ : eiϕ D(ξ) ∈ S forms a full-rank, symplectically integral
                       

lattice.
    Given a generating set as in Eq. (12), we refer to the vector of phases {ϕi }2n i=1 as the
sector of the code. Crucially the sector of a given stabilizer depends on the chosen lattice
generator M = (ξ1 , . . . , ξ2n )T and distinct choices of pairs (M , ϕ) can yield the same
stabilizer. We refer to the choice ϕ = 0 as the trivial sector and note that this choice
specifies a unique stabilizer independent of the chosen generator for every even lattice. In
Section 5 we will be occupied with the study of the set of all stabilizers of this form.
    First let us note a striking feature of GKP codes — they allow for the implementation of
both logical Pauli and Clifford operations by Hamiltonians that are, respectively, degree-1
or degree-2 polynomials in the position and momentum operators.

6 Geometric fault tolerance
Our aim in this section is to prove the geometric fault tolerance conjecture given by Gottes-
man and Zhang in Ref. [8] for the case of GKP Pauli and Clifford operations. The general
version of the conjecture reads as follows.
Conjecture 1 (Gottesman and Zhang). Fault-tolerant logical gates can always be expressed
as arising from monodromies of an appropriate fiber bundle with a flat projective connection.
    We prove that the set of Gaussian unitary operators U G induces a flat projective
connection on the trivial vector bundle over the GKP moduli space MGKP whose fiber over
any point C ∈ MGKP is the space R2n of displacement operators. The parallel transport
maps of the connection take values within U G and act on elements of the fiber via adjoint
action D(ξ) 7→ U (t)D(ξ)U † (t). As logical Pauli operators are displacements and hence
elements of the fiber, the logical action on codewords induced by parallel transport along
any path is fully determined. We split the proof into two separate Lemmas below.

Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2 constitute a proof of Theorem 1.1 and hence the geometric fault

our knowledge, this constitutes the first explicit example of geometric fault tolerance in a
multi-mode bosonic error correction code; see, however, also our separate paper Ref. [9]
that treats the single-mode case using algebraic tools. The main difference between our
construction and those used to prove the conjecture for the case of transversal gates and
a set of topological gates in Ref. [8] is that we do not explicitly construct a connection on
a vector bundle over a submanifold within the Grassmanian GrK (H), the manifold of all
dimension-K subspaces of a Hilbert space. Instead, the manifold upon which we construct
a connection is one consisting of GKP stabilizer groups. The difference stems from the fact
that GKP code-states are formally of infinite energy and hence do not form a well-defined
subspace, necessitating an indirect description through the stabilizer group.
    While we have exclusively dealt with the idealized infinite energy versions of GKP codes,
we expect our main results, Lemmas 6.2 and 6.1, to carry over to the finite energy setting.
In the finite energy setting the GKP manifold MGKP needs to be replaced by a manifold
of approximation dependent finite-energy codes. Additionally, while we have focused on
gates implemented by Gaussian unitary operations, such gates can in general deform the
envelopes of finite energy states, and would need to be replaced by explicitly envelope
preserving operations [23, 24]. We leave the detailed development of such a formulation to
future work.


7 Conclusion
We have investigated the class of GKP quantum error correcting codes from a geometric
point of view. In particular, we have determined the moduli space of all multi-mode GKP
codes and formally established it as a bundle over the moduli space of symplectically
integral lattices. We have shown that this bundle is non-trivial and labeled its connected
components by a unique type, each corresponding to a canonical decomposition of the
encoded logical system into qudits. Furthermore, we have shown that the well-known
Gaussian implementations of logical Pauli and Clifford operations on GKP codes induce a
flat projective connection on the GKP moduli space, proving for these operations the fault
tolerance conjecture of Gottesman and Zhang [8]. Our work constitutes the first proof of
the conjecture for a set of continuous variable codes.
    We believe that our classification of GKP codes will be a useful tool aiding in the
practical implementation of multi-mode codes and hope that this work can stimulate addi-
tional interest in the relationship between quantum error correction and geometry. Future
work could investigate different types of error-correcting codes within the same framework.
Of particular interest here would be to understand the geometry of the space of concate-
nated GKP codes, as this class of codes provides an embedding of natively qubit- or qudit
stabilizer codes into multi-mode GKP codes [15] and the respective GKP moduli spaces
are expected to encode specific characteristics, such as the existence of transversal gates.
Another important avenue for future exploration is extending the geometric perspective to

A Vector and fiber bundles
Here we give a short and non-rigorous introduction to the concept of vector bundles and,
more generally, fiber bundles. The introduction is intended for readers with little or no
prior exposure to bundle theory and omits some technicalities. We refer the interested
reader to Refs. [12, 13] for more detailed treatments.
    One of the most commonly occurring objects in physics are functions f : B → C on a
manifold B. Such a function assigns to every point x ∈ B a value within the vector space
C, or, more generally, within some other vector space V . In certain settings, however, it
turns out to be more natural to assign to x ∈ B not values within one fixed vector space,
but within different vector spaces Vx , one for each point x ∈ B. This assignment of vector
spaces, one to each point, gives rise to the notion of a vector bundle.

Definition A.1 (Vector Bundle). A vector bundle is a pair of topological spaces B and T
together with an onto, continuous map p : T → B, such that the pre-image p−1 (x) of any
x ∈ B, has the structure of a vector space.

    One usually refers to the space T as the total space and to B as the base space. The
pre-image p−1 (x) of x ∈ B is called the fiber over x. The generalized notion of a function,
which assigns to each x ∈ B a value within the fiber over it is called a section.
    Simple examples of vector bundles are the cartesian products B × V of the base space
with a vector space, together with the natural projection (b, v) 7→ b. Such bundles are
called trivial bundles. Another natural example of a vector bundle is the tangent bundle of
a manifold, where the fiber over each point in the base space is simply the space of vectors
tangent to that point of the manifold. The main example of a vector bundle discussed
within the main text is the case where B parametrizes a family of error-correcting codes
and where the fiber over each point is the the space R2n of displacement operators.
    One of the most immediate consequences of the vector bundle construction is that one
cannot immediately compare the values of a section at different points within the base
space, as they assume values within different vector spaces. In order to compare two
vectors, they must lie within the same vector space, and one introduces the notion of a
connection to enable this. A connection mathematically describes the action of transporting
a vector along the fibers over a path γ : [0, 1] → B. We give the following definition, which,
though weaker than the usual definition of a connection, is sufficient for the purpose of
this introduction.

Definition A.3 (Flatness of a connection). A connection is called flat if the transport

    In particular flatness implies that the transport map assigned to a contractible loop

generally, however, one might want to allow target spaces other than vector spaces. Drop-

of a fiber bundle. While there is no general requirement for all fibers of a bundle to be
copies of some reference fiber, this is the case throughout this work. In this case case one
refers to the reference fiber as the standard fiber.
